correctness.rationale: Exact centrally symmetric circumradius/leverage identity; Gaussian Stiefel representation; chi-square near-zero expansion; multinomial Poisson limits squeezed via spectral convergence; exponentially small low-eigenvalue event and uniform chi-square-minimum moments; explicit inclusion-exclusion and verified octahedral antiderivative. Computation supports rather than establishes infinite claims.

evidence: Böröczky–Henk Theorem 1.1 concerns expected k-face counts for fixed projected dimension.
Donoho–Tanner main theorem and full sections concern survival rates of projected faces and neighborliness, not radius endpoints.
The September 2026 source abstract concerns high-probability upper/lower bounds for random section diameters, not this exact projection-radius distribution.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Face-count and neighborliness thresholds do not determine Euclidean lengths of the projected original vertices. A central hyperplane section is neither the orthogonal projection nor its polar without a change of body/functional; the cited section result is therefore not stronger coverage.

evidence: The section result normalizes diameter deficit by n sqrt(log n), whereas projection with fixed codimension one has n^3 loss, using a different random body.
The inradius is reciprocal to a cube-section circumradius; the proposed circumradius is directly a minimum leverage score and a distinct functional.
Projection-face-count expectations do not specify the normal-coordinate minima or their marked point process.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: No inspected source proves a statement that logically implies the announced endpoint process or its exact C3 marginal. The Gaussian small-ball expansion is classical and explicitly credited as the probability mechanism; the geometric transfer and full spectrum are narrowly asserted.

evidence: The radial deficits equal scaled minima of Haar normal-space row leverage scores, and their Gaussian proxy is the low tail of independent chi-square variables.
The published section-diameter law is an order-statistic ratio involving min and max absolute normal coordinates; the shadow loss uses only the normal leverage minimum.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Equivalently this is a Poisson extreme point process for the smallest diagonal entries of a fixed-rank random orthogonal projector. We searched that geometric phrasing and the cross-polytope framing; no ranked result stated this process. The mathematical probabilistic reduction does not by itself prove novelty.

evidence: The published octahedral inradius law is exact but measures the largest inscribed disk; the new closed form measures the minimum containing disk.
The publicly indexed published-finding corpus result for octahedral section diameter is for C3 intersected with a plane, not projected into a plane.
exact_database_or_table.reasoning: Neither exact geometry table or closed law found enumerates the same projection circumradius CDF, and the indexed exact inradius is not sufficient to recover it. Absence of an indexed table is not a proof of uniqueness.

originality.rationale: Direct full-text primary comparisons show existing projected crosspolytope face counts and section-diameter law do not imply the fixed-codimension shadow-radius Poisson process; the published octahedron projection-inradius CDF does not imply the distinct circumradius law. Possible unindexed leverage-minimum equivalents remain a priority risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed statistical literature on smallest Haar leverage scores may cover the same Poisson process under different terminology.
The recent 2026 general random-section paper was only inspected at abstract level, but section versus projection differences reduce direct coverage risk.
The 1997 relevant preprint displays month only, not a verified day; the recorded focal first-public day belongs to the separate 2006 arXiv source.

value.rationale: A full codimension-indexed Poisson endpoint spectrum of a fundamental high-dimensional convex polytope has geometric interest beyond isolated first moments. The sharp scaling \(n^{1+2/q}\), nontrivial Weibull-shape changes, all-positive-moment convergence, and exact finite octahedral normalization give quantitative, reusable random-shadow geometry. Not an arbitrary slice of a known tabulation.
